stops.name: Lobos, the adobe rancho on the pampa
stops.campa: On the eighth of October a boy is born in a low adobe rancho at Lobos, on the flat green immensity of the Buenos Aires pampa, natural son of Mario Tomás Perón and the criolla Juana Sosa. The gauchos come and go across the plain; the horizon is one unbroken line. He is baptized Juan Domingo. Later chroniclers will dispute the year and the place, whispering 1893, whispering Roque Pérez, but the register at Lobos names the day, and the day is kept. From this humble ground the man who will move millions is lifted into the world.
stops.quote: Nací en un hogar de clase media, mi padre era criador de ovejas.
stops.quote_source: Juan Perón, autobiographical recollections ('Del poder al exilio')

stops.name: Río Gallegos, the estancias of the far south
stops.campa: The family embarks on the ship Santa Cruz for the ends of the earth. Mario Tomás, restless, seeks fortune in sheep on the wind-scoured estancias near Río Gallegos: Chaok-Aike, Kamesa-Aike, Coy-Aike, names the Tehuelche gave the land. The five-year-old learns cold that cuts and a sky that never ends. Here the pampa's boy becomes a child of Patagonia, riding before he can well walk, watching the shearers and the peones. The frontier teaches him the first lesson of his life: that the men who do the labor are the men who hold the country up.

stops.name: Camarones, the port town and the justice of the peace
stops.campa: In February the family moves north to Camarones, a huddle of houses on the Chubut coast where the sea batters a rocky bay. Mario Tomás serves as juez de paz, dispensing rough justice among the settlers and the natives; the boy watches his father weigh disputes and knows the shape of authority up close. He roams the meseta on horseback, learns to shoot, learns the silence of great distances. Later, when he is master of a nation, Perón will say the Patagonian frontier made him: that there a man was measured only by what he could do.

stops.name: Sierra Cuadrada, the estancia La Porteña
stops.campa: The family gains its own land at last: La Porteña, a stone-and-adobe house in the Sierra Cuadrada, inland from Comodoro Rivadavia. Wind, sheep, and the great arid plateau. Every summer of his boyhood the boy returns here from the schools of the capital, and the bond with this land never breaks; decades later, as president, he will nearly move here with Evita. The Patagonian summers forge in him the endurance of a mountain man and a deep, wordless conviction that the interior, the forgotten south, is the true heart of the country.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Colegio Militar de la Nación
stops.campa: On the first of March the tall, athletic boy from Patagonia enters the Colegio Militar de la Nación, a scholarship won for him carrying him past the gate. He is a natural: fencer, boxer, gymnast, a rider already hardened by the south. Discipline, hierarchy, the science of command: these become his native tongue. On the thirteenth of December 1913 he graduates subteniente of infantry, forty-third of sixty-four in the 38th promotion. The army will be his home, his school, and his instrument for four decades; the boy of the estancias has become an officer of the Republic.

stops.name: Paraná, the young lieutenant of the 12th Infantry
stops.campa: The new subteniente takes his first post with the 12th Infantry Regiment at Paraná on the river. He drills conscripts drawn from the poorest of the provinces, and among these barefoot boys of the interior he learns something the salons of Buenos Aires never taught: how the humble Argentine lives, what he suffers, what he is owed. The officer discovers a talent for winning men: for being loved by those beneath him without loss of command. It is the seed of everything: the conductor of masses is first the captain who is followed gladly.

stops.name: Campo de Mayo, instructor at the School of Non-Commissioned Officers
stops.campa: At the vast garrison of Campo de Mayo Perón serves as instructor at the Escuela de Suboficiales through the early twenties, teaching the sergeants who are the true spine of the army. He writes manuals; he masters the art of explaining, of making the complex simple, of speaking so that a plain man understands and obeys with pride. The suboficiales are drawn from the people, and they will remember him. When the crisis comes in 1945, it is this bond, the officer beloved of the ranks, that helps carry him from prison to the balcony.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, professor at the Escuela Superior de Guerra
stops.campa: Captain, then major, Perón teaches military history at the Escuela Superior de Guerra, the War College, through the thirties. He studies the great captains: the Napoleonic wars, the strategy of concentration, the theory of the offensive. And he writes on Argentine military history and on the frontier campaigns. In these years the tactician becomes a thinker of national organization, brooding on the state, on discipline, on the mobilization of a whole people. The professor of strategy is quietly assembling the doctrine that will one day be called Justicialismo.

stops.name: Rome, arrival of the military observer
stops.campa: In February Perón arrives in Rome as military observer to Mussolini's Italy, sent to study the alpine troops and the new corporate state. He is forty-three, a lieutenant colonel, keen-eyed and hungry to learn. He walks the imperial capital under its fascist banners and studies how a whole nation is being organized: labor, capital, and state braided into a single corporate body. What he sees will haunt his own doctrine: the Third Position, neither capitalist nor communist, the organized community. But he comes above all as a soldier of the mountains, and to the mountains he goes.

stops.name: Merano, the Tridentina Alpine Division
stops.campa: In July Perón joins the Alpine Division Tridentina at Merano and Bolzano in the Dolomites, the very valleys through which, a century and a half before, Goethe crossed toward Italy. Here the Argentine officer trains with the Alpini, the elite mountain infantry, on rock and ice and glacier. He climbs, he skis, he lives among the crack troops of the Alps and earns their respect. The endurance of the Patagonian boyhood serves him now; the man who rode the Sierra Cuadrada takes to the high peaks as if born to them.

stops.name: Aosta, the Alpine School and the roof of the Alps
stops.campa: At the Scuola di Alpinismo of Aosta, beneath the giants of Mont Blanc and the Gran Paradiso, Perón completes his training as a mountain officer and is decorated by his superiors as a distinguished alpino. He also attaches to the Pinerolo division in Piedmont. These are the finest professional months of his soldiering: to master the highest and hardest ground, among the best troops of a European army. He will carry the Cóndor de los Andes, the mountain-troop badge, and the memory of these peaks all his life.

stops.name: Rome, Piazza Venezia: the day of the declaration of war
stops.campa: On the tenth of June Perón stands in the Piazza Venezia among the roaring crowd as Mussolini appears on the balcony and hurls Italy into the war. The Argentine watches the theatre of the balcony, the ocean of upturned faces, the single voice commanding the multitude, and something is fixed in him forever. He has seen how a leader and a people become one body across a square. Five years and four months later, from a balcony over the Plaza de Mayo, he will answer that vision with one of his own, and the descamisados will roar back.
